t: LeetCode 1816 - Truncate Sentence: Keep the First K Words
o: Words are separated by exactly one space with no leading or trailing whitespace, so the k-th word ends either right before the k-th space or at the end of the string. Example 1 keeps Hello how are you and drops Contestant; example 3 has k equal to the total word count, so nothing is cut and the sentence comes back unchanged. The guarantee that k never exceeds the word count removes all boundary hand-wringing: a truncation always exists. Both a library-flavored solution (split, slice, join) and a scan-based solution (find where the k-th space sits and slice) fit comfortably in the tiny limits.
k: Because separators are single spaces, the answer is simply the prefix of the string ending just before the k-th space (or the whole string).
split/slice/join solves it in one line; counting spaces while scanning avoids allocating the word list.

a.i: Split the sentence on spaces, take the first k tokens and rejoin them with single spaces. It mirrors the problem statement directly and is the version to write first while talking.
s: Split s into words on the space separator
Join them with single spaces and return
a.t: O(n) - every character is copied a constant number of times.
a.sp: O(n) - the split materializes all words.

a.n: Approach 2: Scan for the K-th Space
a.i: Walk the string once, decrementing k at every space; the moment k hits zero, the current index is exactly where the truncated sentence must end. If the scan finishes first, k covered all words and the original string is returned untouched.
s: Iterate i over the characters of s
When k reaches 0 return the prefix s[0..i)
If the loop completes, return s unchanged
a.t: O(n) - a single left-to-right pass that may exit early.
a.sp: O(1) extra - only the returned slice is allocated.

w: In an interview say the split-and-join idea, then note you can do it without building the token list by hunting for the k-th space - that shows you see strings as slices, not just arrays. Pitfalls: assuming a trailing space exists after the last word (there is none, hence the fall-through return), and off-by-one errors between word index and space index. This problem rarely gets follow-ups beyond handling arbitrary whitespace or returning the dropped remainder.
